a: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a tree data structure where each node has at most two children, and for any given node, all values in its left subtree are less than the node's value, while all values in its right subtree are greater. This property enables efficient O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion operations on average. In Java, a BST is typically implemented with a Node class as an inner class and a BST class that manages the root reference and exposes public methods. Each Node contains a value (often using generics with Comparable or a Comparator for ordering) and references to left and right children. The most straightforward way to implement BST operations is recursively, since the tree structure naturally lends itself to recursive algorithms. For insertion, you compare the value to the current node; if it is less, you recursively insert into the left subtree; if greater, into the right subtree; if equal, you may either ignore the duplicate or handle it based on your design. For search, you follow the same comparison logic until you either find the value or reach a null reference, indicating the value is not in the tree. Deletion is more complex, with three cases: deleting a leaf (simply remove it), deleting a node with one child (replace it with its child), and deleting a node with two children (find the in-order successor or predecessor, copy its value, and recursively delete that node). Traversal methods — in-order (left, root, right) which produces sorted output, pre-order, and post-order — are also commonly implemented. Additional useful methods include finding the minimum and maximum values, checking the height of the tree, and validating whether the tree maintains BST properties. For a robust implementation, you should also consider whether the tree allows duplicates, how to handle null values, and the potential for the tree to become unbalanced, which degrades performance to O(n) in the worst case. Self-balancing variants like AVL trees or Red-Black trees address this limitation.
